image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Scatter plot** with a **fitted trend line**
- Includes one large overall scatter plot and a row of **small-multiple scatter plots** for specific crime categories

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: five smaller scatter plots labeled **Assaults, Robberies, Murders, Burglaries, Larcenies**
- **Reference lines**: vertical and horizontal zero lines
- **Trend lines**: one in the main panel and one in each small panel
- No stacking

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Change in undocumented immigrants (per 100,000 people) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Change in violent crimes (per 100,000 people) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis in the main scatter plot |
| Crime category (Assaults, Robberies, Murders, Burglaries, Larcenies) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting / small-multiple panel titles |
| Change in crime rate for each faceted category (per 100,000 people) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis within each small-multiple panel |
| Metropolitan area (180 metro areas) | Categorical/nominal | Individual points/marks (one dot per metro area) |

Notes:
- Point color appears uniform and does **not** encode a separate variable.
- The trend lines and zero lines are analytical/reference elements, not additional data variables.

comments.raw_comment:
Title: Back 2 Africa. 
The title is a play on the fact that most of the high-fertility nations are in Africa and have been for some time.

The largest determining factor for high fertility rates is economic growth and development.
When we were mainly an agriculturally-based society, farming required a lot more physical labor and hands to do this on each farm.  As we became Industrialized, families needed less kids. And now, as a Technologically-driven economy, kids have become more of a cost and financial burden; just ask the South Koreans (they have the lowest fertility rate in the world).

Most of the 1st World Nations have been undergoing fertility crises for some time, including the U.S, Britain, China, Russia, Japan, Korea, and Germany, and France.
And this crises was intensified by the widespread development of the birth control pill.
What has kept depopulation at bay for a number of developed nations, including the U.S (my home), Germany, England, and France, has been immigration.
In the U.S, we’ve used immigrants as a cheap source of labor, but also as a source investment.

But most importantly, we’ve used them for growth. You see, if we don’t maintain the replacement rate, our economic growth, our retirement system, our labor force, our education system, our retail markets, and a lot of other parts of our product-driven economy will all start to fall apart rather quickly.

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?- From looking at this graph, I noticed that as mentioned in the caption, the Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is below the replacement rate, except for certain African regions and the Middle East. The replacement rate is crucial because it indicates the number of children a family can have relative to the current population, ensuring population sustainability.

2. What do you wonder?- I wonder what lies ahead for us, if there is anything. This may sound pessimistic, but I have wondered about this before. Living to an age that feels rather precarious is becoming more common. Living on the edge of existence seems, honestly, much worse than embracing the inevitable end. I feel like to truly feel young, you should act like you are. Letting your age define you is what enforces the idea that age should determine the way you act and that you’re getting old. I think about how we all could feel forever young if we become more aware that tomorrow isn’t promised.

3. How does this relate to you and your community?- It makes sense to me to think that this impacts both me and my community deeply, given that this is our home, the Earth. Earth is our everything. It is the only home to us. The observable population spikes indicate a rapid growth in this space we call home. I question the habitability of having such a vast population on this planet with limited space that we call our home.

4. Unveiling Earth's Demographic Drama: Navigating Overpopulation Trends!

comments.raw_comment: When looking at the graph I notice that Hong Kong has the lowest fertility rate of .7 children per two people. I wonder what factors has induced the fertility rates in Hong Kong to plummet that low. Additionally, I wonder why African countries like Niger, Mali and Niger have the highest fertility rates ranging from 5 children per two people to 6.8 children. My hypothesis is that age structure plays a big role in the fertility rates in these African countries. This relates to my community because the United States, the country I live in, has a fertility rate of 1.7 children per two people which is below the replacement fertility rate of 2.1 children. A catchy headline for this graph could be "How Declining Fertility Rates Around the World Predict a Small Global Population of 2 Billion People in the Next 300 Years."

comments.raw_comment:
What Will Countries Do About Low Fertility Rates?

Looking at the graph, I notice that many countries have birth rates below the replacement fertility. These countries are generally very developed countries such as South Korea, Japan, Germany, and even the United States. The countries with higher fertility rates are less developed countries, typically in Africa. Low population levels can cause massive issues in the economies of countries and the workforce. This makes me wonder, what are countries doing to help stop this issues? Is this a problem that can be completely prevented? This relates to me because the declining population influences the policies governments put into place. Support systems for the elderly such as social security will not exist for much longer because the increasing burden it is putting on young people.

comments.raw_comment:
Does Infertility Help or Hurt Our Countries?

As I look at this graph, I notice a significant change in the fertility rates between different countries. As of today, fertility rates are rather low in areas like Hong Kong, China, Italy, and India (places below the replacement fertility line). However, the graph shows that in areas like Nigeria, Mali, and Niger the fertility rates are much larger. In the United States (a fertility rate of 1.7) and many other countries, there is an outstanding number of people. These places are continuously becoming overpopulated, so I find the low fertility rates in this graph quite surprising. 

The surprisingly low fertility rates makes me wonder what is causing them to become so low in the United States and some of the other areas with low rates. Is it one’s age or lifestyle that affects one’s fertility rates? And why are other places like Africa and Mali showing higher rates? I don’t think this decreasing rate of fertility will affect the United States terribly, at least in the beginning. The United States is already so overpopulated and I feel as though it will eventually be very hard to provide everyone with the resources they need. This decreasing fertility rate may help even out the amount of people within the United States, which isn’t a bad thing. I actually think this decreasing rate could be a good thing. And who knows, these decreasing rates could take an unexpected turn and start increasing.

Second, The note about where most people live  implies that a significant portion of the global population live in countries with declining birth rates. Last but not least, the concept of replacement fertility is highlighted, with a suggested threshold of about 2.1. Countries like China(1.2), India(2.0), and Italy (1.3) have a total fertility rate below this replacement level. This implies that, on average, these countries are not having enough births to replace their existing population over the long term.

comments.raw_comment:
- I noticed a disparity in fertility rates between Global South nations, particularly in Africa, where rates remain relatively high, and developed countries, where fertility rates are often below replacement levels, such as in the U.S. However, I was not shocked by China or India having below replacement fertility levels. Additionally, these rates exhibit significant variations across different population sizes.
- I wonder what specific factors contribute to the higher fertility rates in many African countries compared to the lower rates in developed nations.
- This data directly affects both my community and me, especially now that our society is dealing with the repercussions of Roe v. Wade in the U.S. Many women are in a state of vulnerability due to limitations on their choice of fertility. This trend could become critical over time. However, it should be acknowledged that with populations in the U.S. already experiencing below replacement fertility, it instills fear of what will happen for future populations. This fear arises when you dwell on the possible socioeconomic consequences with future populations, especially if these populations continue to decline.
- "Fertility Frontiers: Insights into Global Fertility Trends and Variances"

comments.raw_comment:
Not Baby Boomers.

I think this is mainly a cultural “issue”.  I say that because I don’t think it really is an issue but I also because the cultural importance of family differs a lot between regions.  In America, after World War II, we know that the baby boom occurred– in which the population grew immensely.  Since then most people have been having fewer and fewer children.  Most parents I know have1-3 kids.  The cultural climate is changing in America… especially as the cost of living increases.  One thing being specifically affected by this is the cost of housing, healthcare, and childcare…which are all very important in raising a child.  Many women have to quit their jobs in order to stay home with the kids which obviously means less income for the family.

comments.raw_comment: Notably I notice that outside of the just Sub-Saharan Africa, much of North Africa like Egypt, Libya, and Morocco always have fertility rates well above replacement fertility rates. Another notable outlier is Israel which has a fertility rate of 3, despite it being in similar socioeconomic status of countries like the UK and US, which have less fertility rates. As a American I wonder mostly whether continued economic growth will create a desire to increase fertility rates, something which really isn't a topic of discussion in political matters. I also wonder whether the high fertility rates in Northern Africa is caused by political destabilization, like the Araba Spring, something that has certainly happened in Venezuela.  A really catchy headline for the graph would something like "The perilous future for future humans".

comments.raw_comment:
Seeing the graph, I notice that the bubbles as you go down the map have smaller and smaller child per woman ratio. I’ve noticed that countries at the bottom of the map, are more developed, and the rate of children per woman goes down. For example in the US, the rate of children is 1.7 per woman, because in the United States, children don't go straight out to the workforce and, unlike undeveloped countries, teens/ adults get paid a substantially greater amount than people in other countries. Although in other countries you may be able to work as a young child, America has placed The Federal Child Labor Law in place so children under the age of 14 can't work, but kids in other countries aren't so fortunate.

As you go further up the graph, places like Somalia (6.3) and Mali (6.0), the birth to woman ratio is increasingly higher than many developed countries. But a depressing truth is why the birth rates are so high in specific countries, as a woman has more children, they grow up and start working at young ages, making money for corporations that use those kids to make more money. In those countries though, they do not have laws to protect those children or teens from being unpaid in the workforce. This causes many deaths in children in those specific countries. And with the increasing demand to move to a country where the birth rates are lower and everyone who immigrated to the United States, we might experience a population influx, causing the American population to go down.

comments.raw_comment: This Graph shows where each country falls due to the amount of children a woman has. For example, Niger is at the top because the average amount of kids a woman has is 6.8. But near the bottom is Hong Kong because they only have 0.7 children per woman. The U.S. falls somewhat toward the end. We have 1.7 children per woman. I have one sister and that's it so we fall close to the average. And most of my friends have either one or two siblings max. So this graph makes some sense. The Graph also says that most people now live in places with low-replacement fertility. This means a lot of people live in places where the amount of children per woman is very low. That's why the end of the graph is red because below the red line are the people who have less than 2 kids. I’m not sure why people now live in these areas. It might have something to do with the economy, popular trends, the conditions of where you live, or maybe even the weather. But we don't know that yet.

comments.raw_comment:
In this graph, it has become clear that each dot represents a woman in a geographical location as well as the average number of children they have. These numbers are declining. Countries in Africa such as Niger, Nigeria and Chad have a much higher fertility rate than let's say China or the United States. From what I have learned, women in African and other regions nearby begin motherhood at a younger age, allowing for them to have more children. Also, it is important to know that many African countries value having larger families, which may have started to counteract the deaths of so many young children due to the lack of necessary resources. 
            On the other side of the graph, even the countries with the most number of people are the lowest in fertility rates and I have reason to believe that it is because of overpopulation. If you look on a map, it is simple to see how China and India are not very large countries, and yet, they still have the highest population. So imagine if that population kept rising, then there would be no room left for anyone. The citizens may not have enough resources for themselves to live off of, yet again for another child. 
    I wonder how overpopulation became such an issue and what different governments are doing about it. I also wonder what governments are doing about the decreased fertility.

comments.raw_comment: First when I toke a glance at this graph, I just expected it to be about how something in the world is expanding. Not knowing that it is more depth than that. Looking at this graph I have started to notice that the circles are the amount of total fertility rate. Once I scrolled down I saw many big red circles that represented India and China. It's truly crazy to think that the places that have the most fertility rate are India and China. “What about the US?” Don’t we have a lot of people also, this honestly doesn't make any sense. I started to scroll down even more until I reached the point where I saw writers talking about the population will reaching a peak in about 10 million people around 2085. “Crazy” that's the first thought that came to mind when I saw the date “2085”, that's in 62 years. Frankly it's scary to think that the population will only be increasing as time goes on. I wonder what happens when there comes a point where the population can’t get any bigger. “What will happen then?”. Will we have to start moving away or what? On the other hand, it's kind of interesting to think about what the world will be looking like once 2085 hits. As the population increasing over time it will be fascinating to watch society build.

comments.raw_comment: I notice that many countries in the Global South, especially African countries, retain higher fertility rates while many countries considered developed have lower fertility rates and especially rates below the replacement rate. These rates vary a lot across the total population size. The way that fertility is being defined here is quite multifaceted. I wonder how much of this trend has to do with the choice of AFAB people to have children vs. access to healthcare and other environmental and sociopolitical factors. Especially in the aftermath of Roe V. Wade in the U.S., this element of choice in fertility is even more vulnerable for women/AFAB people. It’s interesting to think about whether this trend will change if a similar policy isn’t reinstated in the U.S. As a population ages, this also has effects on the expectation for work and on the overall social and political beliefs of the country. A common criticism of political figures (members of Congress, the House, etc.) is that they don't represent the U.S. population because they skew older. As populations age, it might take longer for certain beliefs to change or shift.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph depicts total fertility and infertility rates in the population. The circles sizes grow larger depending on the population of the specific country. I notice how Niger has the highest fertility rate and China has the lowest fertility rates. I wonder if the fertility rates have to deal with the size of the population. Niger has a smaller population compared to China yet has higher fertility rate. This could be because China made the one child per family rule. I wonder why the rates are lower for countries that have the most people because you would expect them to be fertile due to the large population. This could be because of the increase of women working in the workforce and not having the time to raise children which led to a decrease in fertility rates. This relates to me and my community because I am a daughter, granddaughter, cousin, sister, and niece and have a smaller family. I eventually want to start a family of my own some day and the issues of infertility is a scare that many women in my community and across the globe have to go through. Also, I live in the United States and our population has decreased over the years a lot which could be because of the high abortion rates. 
My Super Duper Catchy Title: Baby I'm Yours

In larger countries which have dense populations we observe declining fertility rates which are below the replacement fertility line. I believe that this is a result of an increase in women being part of the workforce, thereby having less of a desire and opportunity to nurture a traditional family life. However, some countries have external variables that are impacting their fertility rates, such as China who have implemented the one child policy. I’m curious if we’ll see an increase in population, since these third world countries now have the opportunity to manufacture goods for first world countries thereby contributing to GDP and enhancing the resources available to the people in that country. For example, Nike now outsources their manufacturing to Vietnam which provides more employment opportunities and an increase in revenue in the country. This is relevant to my community and I because I live in the United States and our population is declining which may affect my generation and future generations because there will be less people to contribute to society politically, socially, and economically.

comments.raw_comment:
Looking at today’s, “What’s Going On in This Graph?”, I've had a few thoughts and noticed some things I thought helped me understand more about the graph. I wasn’t aware that fertility rates were something that was measured, and when I did see the data and numbers, I didn’t really know what all of them meant. After getting a clear understanding of what the numbers and circle sizes meant, I have a clue as to why maybe many of the more densely populated and developed countries have lower fertility rates.

If you take a look at the graph as a whole, you notice that the graph takes, sort of, a teardrop shape. The more fertile countries at the top, less fertile countries at the bottom. The graph is bigger at the bottom due to many developed, densely populated, bigger countries occupying that space. I would like to say that the countries at the bottom of the graph are at the bottom due to not feeling the need to reproduce, and probably the growing number of people not wanting or even hating the idea of having a child, but I wouldn’t say this is bad. It’s quite understandable why people don’t want to have kids nowadays. Our Earth is severely overpopulated, danger is always on the rise, and a lot of people really aren’t cut out to have kids. Though this chart is interesting and demonstrates how what kind of environment you live in can influence reproduction, I don’t think these numbers are anything to be worried about for now.

1. What do you notice?
-From the graph, I noticed that many countries in Africa have the highest-fertility rates. Also, I noticed that most of the countries that have low fertility rates are first world. 

2. What do you wonder? 
-Since the U.S. is below replacement fertility, I wonder if this can cause bigger issues as years go on. I also wonder how people in Africa manage to take care of their families sufficiently. They have a high population and high fertility rates, so they have more kids, and more things to take care of.

-This relates to my community because the U.S. has a very low fertility rate. This can affect everything around me, for example, if there's low fertility rates, that means there's a lower population (or less people), which can lead to a greater demand for certain jobs.

The age of marriage for women has also increased and is higher than in most developing nations. There are also a lot more women in the workforce and less women have the time to be homemakers.

I notice that countries in Africa have very high fertility rates compared to all other continents and countries. Niger has the highest, with each women having 6.8 children on average. I also notice that smaller countries have higher fertility rates as compared to large countries like China or America. I wonder what the future of Africa could be like if the population keeps growing. Will poverty increase or will some countries become powerful and prominent in the world? I also wonder if the new generations of Gen-Z or Gen-Alpha will change these rates, whether increasing or decreasing. This relates to me and my community because I know a lot of people my age who do not want to have children, and it makes me think of the future for my children and whether they will live in a growing, prosperous world with successful leaders. 

'Information of fertility decreasing scares nations world wide"

The graph shows the average fertility rates in countries around the world. The countries are represented by bubbles that vary in size, with the smaller ones having a smaller population, and vice versa. Most of the big bubbles (countries with large populations) are below the replacement fertility rate, which is the rate of reproduction at which the population stabilizes. I wonder why bigger and more powerful countries like America, Australia, and Brazil have lower birth rates. Maybe it's because people are more focused on earning a living in those areas, and have less time to raise a family. 
The caption of the graph caught my attention. It states that the human population will peak at 10 billion in my lifetime, and then eventually stabilize at around 2 billion. That means that I'll live in a time period that has the most humans ever. 
Headline: POPULATION PLUMMETING OR POPPING UP?

comments.raw_comment:
This graph exhibits population size and comparison to the total fertility rate. In the graph, it is shown that Niger has a population of 100 million and has a total fertility rate of 6.8. Niger is located in West Africa and is one of the poorest countries in the world. Therefore because of their lack of advanced technologies and good health care, they probably have a higher infant mortality rate So, if they have six kids they can assume that a few of them will die at birth if not in the first few months of their lives. In addition in less developed countries like Niger, it is more socially acceptable to have more kids. Because of their lack of education women could have kids at an earlier age therefore producing more of them. In addition, the kids can go to work at very young ages so they can help provide income for the family. On the other hand, populations like China have implemented anti-natalist policies to control overpopulation. The previous one-child policy and the current two-child policy in China, enforced by the government, have resulted in lower fertility rates. However, these fertility rates are below the replacement rate of 2.1. This could negatively affect a population because the dependency ratio would be high on older people. This could also have a negative effect on economic development because the younger population will not be able to support the older population. I wonder how China is handling this issue they are facing.
“The Future is Babies”

comments.raw_comment:
This graph provides a visual representation of fertility rates throughout different countries and how they are related. The graph is characterized by various bubbles in different colors and sizes representing the number of children, on average, per woman in each bubble's designated country. Closer to the top of the graph, this number increases, topping it off with the country of Niger with a rate of 6.8 children per woman. As the graph deepens, the fertility rate decreases, reaching countries with “below replacement fertility” such as China, India, the US, and Hong Kong with about 2 or less children per woman. 
         I wonder how this declining fertility rate in the USA will affect us in the future. We are one of the most influential countries in the world, with a fertility rate of only 1.7 children per woman. Will this ever hurt, or help our population of people who are eligible to serve in the military? In the future when we are adults with children of our own, will we have less doctors or firefighters with a possible decrease in the population of people that are able to do it? 
         This graph was very interesting, and it sparked questions that I had never even thought of previously. I would love to learn more about this topic in the future, and how it could affect our lives as we grow older.

comments.raw_comment:
The fertility rate gets lower as countries become more developed, a saddening fact that Demographic Transition Model graphs will always show. Third-world countries like Niger(6.8), Mali(6.0), and most countries in Africa all have a need for kids because their countries aren’t developed yet and therefore kids generate money by working, valuable money that ensures parental survival. It's a logical and necessary decision on their part, it's their means of survival.
      However, other countries like the US(1.7) and Germany(1.5) are in the “Industrial” and “Post-Industrial” stages of the Demographic Transition Model, meaning that they no longer have such a need for children and now have kids because of desire rather than need. However, because their replacement rate is lower than the fertility rate in these countries, like the US, immigrants are essential to replenish the workforce and ensure continuation. When this immigration surge stops we end up with countries like Germany who pay in extreme amounts for foreign workers and try desperately to increase fertility rates. It leads one to wonder, what will happen when all countries end up in the “Post-Industrial” and 1st world stage like Germany and Japan? Will we find a way around it? Or will we go extinct?

Ideally these fertility rates will match the replacement fertility so we can have a stable and healthy population.

comments.raw_comment:
Where the world has stopped and where it keeps growing? 
In the graph we can see that a large amount of the largest countries in the world have fertility rates near or below the replacement fertility line. This includes the U.S., China, India, Russia, Brazil, Japan, Italy, UK, and many more. On the opposite end of the spectrum the top 13 countries are all from Africa: Niger, Somalia, Chad, Dem. Republic of Congo, Central African Republic, Mali, Angola, Nigeria, Burundi, Benin, Burkina Faso, Tanzania, and Gambia. Afghanistan and Mozambique are tied in 14th with a rate of 4.6. And below them is a pool of countries mainly from Africa and two countries that aren’t. What is being shown here is that a large part of the world has stagnated in relation to their fertility rate. The only area that is still sustaining their high fertility rate, from the baby boomer years, is Africa, everywhere else has significantly dropped exempt of a couple of anomalies. This is mainly due to there being far higher placement on the need of child rearing comparatively to rest of the world as it seems that most people no either don’t have the money or care to raise a child. The lower rate in child rearing in these nations can be mainly put towards financial issues and potentially the high use of contraceptives. 
Continues in Replies

Then resulting in a policy to limit the number of children the countries have which can eventually lead to underpopulation. Then this could become a continuous cycle.

comments.raw_comment:
Falling Fertility - The Baby Decline:

- What do you notice?
There is an increasing number of countries with a decreasing fertility rate. Additionally, more developed countries tend to be lower on the graph (below replacement TFR), such as European & North American countries. 

- What do you wonder?
How are these countries moving up and down in accordance to population statistics?
We are also curious as the to predictive fertility rates for the next 50 years.
What are future implications of the population declining due to below replacement fertility?
What is the global total fertility rate?

- How does this relate to you and your community?
US fertility rate is below replacement value, so we will need a younger population to support an increasingly aging population in order to maintain stable economic and governmental support programs (social security, other programs funded by working populations' taxes, etc).
This also speaks towards the shifting power imbalances as a result of globalization between countries of the Global North and Global South.
Lower fertility rates could cause future problems.
This topic inherently ties into women's rights and education, as less educated women are more likely birth more children when they are younger.


As usual, thank you for the interesting prompts! :)
- Ms. Francois 5B AP Language class

I notice that the average number of children varies drastically between different countries. In Nigeria, the average birth rate is about 7 whereas in Hong Kong it is about 1. This is a significant difference. I wonder why women typically have so few children in Hong Kong and so many in Nigeria. I wonder how this high birth rate will affect these two countries. I wonder if it will pose a positive or negative effect. On one hand a high birth rate could supply the country with many people eligible to work, improving the economy. However, on the other hand too large of a population can result in a lack of housing and other necessary resources and potentially lead to increased poverty rates. This relates to my community as the U.S.'s fertility rate is 1.7. At first I was suprised to see how low this statistic is, however I recall hearing about people going on birth strike to help improve the enviornment. I wonder what the birth rate will be when I have children one day and when my children have children, and if the predicted lower birth rates will help the enviornment. 
Bye, Bye High Fertility Rates!

comments.raw_comment:
The graph depicts the average fertility rates in various countries around the world. I noticed that countries in Africa possess the highest average fertility rate such as in Niger, Mali and Nigeria. However, countries that may be considered more developed (or contain developing economies), possess lower fertility rates that fall below the replacement fertility rate at 2.1. This includes countries such as India, China and Italy.   One reason for this may be that people are tending to have fewer children due to the expenses necessary for raising a child. This may apply to China (fertility rate of 1.2) and the United States (fertility rate of 1.7) due to financial concerns. An example of this includes child care, higher education and family leave. I wonder if governments will begin to encourage citizens to have more children by lowering costs in some areas of a country or in providing more affordable healthcare. Also, I wonder how -6 as a total fertility rate of the world relates to people’s view of the importance of family. Is family in countries still considered a main form of support and security as it is valued in countries in Africa? Furthermore, this graph relates to my community as my generation, Generation Z, is currently responsible or is going to become the people that impact the average fertility rates of countries. 

A headline for the graph could be “Declining Fertility Rates Are a Danger to the World”

comments.raw_comment:
First of all, this graph displays the fertility rates of the world: with Niger at the top at 6.8, it would be a major understatement to say that the amount of children born to each woman is excessive and unnecessary, though not surprising. Africa has always historically had the highest fertility rates, mostly due to a lack of access to contraceptives and education, as well as the prevalence of polygamy and adolescent marriages. 
      As this graph shows, most developed countries, including the United States, have lower fertility rates, the majority of them being under the replacement fertility threshold. It’s interesting to note that global birth rates have declined over time, which I believe is mostly due to increases in cost of living and childcare, developments in women’s rights, and urbanization, all of which are particularly high in first world countries.
      What concerns me mostly is how low fertility rates have dropped and how that might affect the population. In some places like Japan and South Korea, the birth rate is so low that schools started shutting down because they couldn’t sustain the costs of the institution. In fact, it was so bad that, at any given moment, there were only one or two children actively attending a class. I genuinely hope that those kinds of circumstances don’t spread to the United States and other developed countries, though there might not be so much hope for us either.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph depicts the fertility rate of countries around the world; the lowest rate being Hong Kong at 0.7 and the highest being Niger at 6.8. The graph also draws a gray dotted line showing the ideal replacement fertility rate, 2.1 children per pair of parents, which would sustain the population shifting from one generation to the next. Interestingly, most major countries fall below the ideal replacement fertility rate. Some of which being the US (1.7), India (2.0), Japan (1.3), the UK (1.6), Germany (1.5), and Russia (1.5). Not so shockingly, China falls low at 1.2 children per set of parents, which was a goal of the old one-child policy. I wonder how this will end up affecting the economy and workforce. More specifically, how will manual labor jobs be affected? As people get older, it gets harder for them to efficiently perform hard physical labor. So, will businesses be negatively impacted if there is less accessibility to younger workers? In my community, small shops tend to rely on teenagers as employees. In years to come, the RFR begins to fall, I am sure these businesses will suffer in getting workers.

“Bye-bye Babies!”

I mean it could be because of the prices going up everywhere. Families just aren't able to afford to have them. However, some other countries like Somalia and Chad have over 6.0 rates. comments.raw_comment: In this graph, it is measuring the total fertility rates in different parts of Africa in comparison with other countries. I noticed that the total fertility rates in parts of Africa are significantly higher than in other parts of the world. Particularly, Niger has the highest total fertility rate of 6.8. I also noticed that the African regions have relatively small populations and that for those regions, the smaller population tends to lead to a greater total fertility rate. On the other hand, other nations have much lower fertility rates which are mostly all below the replacement fertility rate, meaning that their populations still are not stabilized. The city of Hong Kong has a very low total fertility rate of only 0.7. I wonder why that fertility rate is so small in comparison to the African region of Niger which looks like it is compatible in population to Hong Kong. I also wonder why the birth rates in small countries of Africa are higher than countries with greater populations and think this could be due to the higher cost of having children in other countries depicted such as India, China, and Italy compared to African regions. This relates to my community because I live in the U.S. and it has a total fertility rate of 1.7, which is below the replacement fertility. A declining population could greatly affect the economy. My headline for this graph would be: “Could African Countries Out-Populate Other Nations Due to Fertility Rates?”

comments.raw_comment:
Title: A Doomed Population

The graph concerns me.

It shows how most of the world has a below-replacement fertility rate with the exception of some African countries whose rates are 2.0 or above. This means that, confusingly, unlike the U.S., Africa's population is stable and is able to replace more people than it loses.

This sparks the question: Will the U.S., along with other countries, stabilize eventually or continue to decline in population?

It affects my community because over time, there will be less and less of us unless we do something about it. Is the solution to make more babies or lower the mortality rate if that’s even possible at this point? Is there even a solution at all? I guess we’ll find out over time.

comments.raw_comment: This graph depicts the declining fertility rates, an issue occurring worldwide. The only region considered as a “higher-fertility” area is Africa. Niger, Mali, and Nigeria are all located at the top of the graph to represent their high fertility rates. On the other hand, countries like the United States, Italy, Brazil, China, and India are all “below-replacement fertility.” I am curious about China’s very low fertility rates in regards to their high population. Additionally, if every two people have two children, a rate known as replacement fertility, how long would it take for the population to stabilize? This impacts my community because the United States is a below-replacement fertility region, with a rate of 1.7 children per woman. As a result, our population, as well as the economy, may begin suffering in future years. I would title this graph “Global Fertility Rates.”

comments.raw_comment: This graph depicts the declining fertility rates, an issue occurring worldwide. The only region considered as a “higher-fertility” area is Africa. Niger, Mali, and Nigeria are all located at the top of the graph to represent their high fertility rates. On the other hand, countries like the United States, Italy, Brazil, China, and India are all “below-replacement fertility.” I am curious about China’s very low fertility rates in regards to their high population. Additionally, if every two people have two children, a rate known as replacement fertility, how long would it take for the population to stabilize? This impacts my community because the United States is a below-replacement fertility region, with a rate of 1.7 children per woman. As a result, our population, as well as the economy, may begin suffering in future years. I would title this graph “Global Fertility Rates.”

comments.raw_comment:
Population Impact on  Fertility Rates!      PART 1

When going over the fertility graph. I can tell that the graph mainly focuses on two sections and countries in Asia and Africa. I can conclude that countries in Africa have a higher birth rate than countries in Asia. For example Niger, a landlocked country in West Africa has a fertility rate of 6.8% while India, a country in South Asia has a fertility rate of 2.0.  I can also tell from the graph however that the rate has dropped over the years. Not only for Asian countries but for African countries as well.  Countries China and India are now in replacement because the population would stabilize if every two people had two children. Mainly saying the fertility rate is below 2.0

I wonder how this would affect the population. Over the years it's dropping less and less and most countries are in below-replacement fertility.  If the graph continues over the years we might stabilize. How long would it take for the population to realize the significant impact and what it means for us. What I believe surprises me the most and really what I wonder the most is why these countries. Countries in Africa and Asia are the most popular nations in the entire world.

comments.raw_comment:
Title: Fertility Around the World
The graph includes fertility from countries all around the world. Africa has a higher fertility rate. But, America and India have lower fertility rates. This could be due to the food people consume in their countries or environmental conditions. African countries deal with their children dying young, so this could be a possible reason for their fertility rate being so high. They want to have their children survive and are willing to keep reproducing until they achieve that. Countries that are very highly populated mostly have a lower fertility rate, which could be due to the people living there feeling overcrowded and smushed together. I wonder why China has such a low fertility rate since their country seems to be populated normally. I’m not sure if this relates to my community but I could see the US having lower fertility rates which would lead to a decreased population which would cause many problems around the world.

I wonder how it will affect the population if women would have the average patterns of birth within their country. I am also curious as to why it depends on where you live to have a certain amount of children.

This ties to the community because we contribute to the fertility decline. Within time families will begin to grow smaller. This can have a major decrease in the economy with there being less people working.

comments.raw_comment:
1. I notice that the African nations of Nigeria, Mali, and Niger are in high fertility zones. The graph indicates that Africa is the only remaining region with higher fertility. I also see that the fertility rates in China, India, Italy, and Hong Kong are below average. Another thing I noticed was that only nations with a population of one million or more are covered, and also that when you move your mouse over a circle, information about the country and average number of children born to a woman in that country is displayed. 

2. I'm wondering about how long it takes for fertility rates to start declining in a nation and how long it takes to notice a significant impact. I'm also curious as to why the fertility rates are lower in some of the most populous nations, and how they even manage to keep it as low considering the climbing worldwide populations.

3. This affects my community because as we can see, the US is below replacement fertility. This concerns me as we were always known to have a relatively large and steady population, yet we are losing more residents than gaining. It leads me to question whether our communities are truly moving forward or if we are taking a step in the wrong direction.

4.Replacement or Disappearance, Which Direction Are Our Countries Working Towards?

I notice that Niger, Mali, and Nigeria, countries located in Africa, are high-fertility regions. Africa is the only higher-fertility region remaining as shown by the graph. I notice that India, Italy, China, and Hong Kong are below-replacement fertility. Only countries with at least one million people are included.  I notice that when you hover your mouse over a circle, it tells you what country it is and how many children an average woman gives birth to in that specific country. The United States, 1.7 children per woman. 

Wonders:
Why are only countries with at least one million people included? Why is Africa the only higher-fertility region remaining. Why are India, China, Italy, Hong Kong, and other countries below-replacement fertility? How hard it is for the population of a region to stabilize in order to get to a rate of 2.1? Why is 2.1 considered replacement fertility, why can’t it be less? Why is the United States below-replacement fertility?

This relates to my community as the United States is below replacement fertility. I was surprised about this information as I thought that because the United States has a big population (340 million) women would give birth to more children (1.7 fertility rate). This information does not relate to me, but it can be talked about in my school and schools in community.

comments.raw_comment:
1. I noticed two aspects of the graph. The first is the countries with the highest fertility rates are located in Africa. Niger, Mali, and Nigeria all have fertility rates above 5. Secondly, I noticed that highly populated countries including China and India have lower fertility rates than some of the less populated countries. Both China and India have below replacement fertility rates according to the graph.

2. I wonder why countries in Africa have higher fertility rates while the fertility rate has dropped in other countries. I also wonder what factors contribute to the fertility rate of a country.

3. The United States is included as one of the below-replacement fertility countries, meaning that the population would not stabilize regardless if every two people had two children. Fertility rates are decreasing and as a result, the populations are expected to decrease with them. As populations decrease economic growth will likely be reduced which impacts communities all around the world including mine.

4. ''Diminishing Fertility Rates Around The Globe'' would be an appropriate headline for this graph.

3. This relates to my community and me because if the population continues to decline, there will be a lack of work causing the economy to run slower. With fewer children, the older generation will have very little to rely on, and the present generation will have more work on their backs to be the main providers.
4. A Vanishing Future, Fertility Rates Declining!

What do you notice?- I notice from this graph that, as stated in the caption, aside from some African regions and the middle east, the TFR's lower than the replacement rate. I wonder how many benefits or damages this causes to countries above and below the replacement rate. For the countries in Africa, higher population can help with development. In other countries, a reducing population might promote sustainability and economic stability.

This relates to my community since the newer generations in the US, from my perspective and understanding, are not as enthusiastic about having kids because they can be really expensive to raise for the time until they can make money for themselves.

Did you know the fertility rate was so low around the world? A lot more goes into it than you think.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that less developed countries have a trend of high fertility rates while more developed countries have a lower fertility rate. This could be due to the idea that once a country becomes more developed, women have more access to education and have a greater choice in whether they want to have children. As women become more educated and have more choices, they often choose to have fewer children. 

I wonder what systems the more developed countries with lower fertility rates could employ in order to increase their birth rates so that they can maintain a stable population. I also wonder how a declining birth rate could benefit countries like India that have a very high population. The decline in fertility rates could help control an overpopulated country.

This relates to our community because if we continue to have a declining fertility rate in the United States, it could create an economic issue. As the population of the U.S. ages and a declining number of babies born, we as a younger generation could have no social security money given to us when we get older because the older generations will have used up all the money apportioned for future generations.

A possible headline for this graph could be "Maybe Babies Can Fix Some Things"
